G1, paper only, 60 minutes | Review synthetic plant genotypes and quality control without operating equipment, handling samples or using real human data. Complete the six sets of materials below: 15 minutes to check sources and conditions, 15 minutes to calculate allele proportions, 20 minutes to fill in three draft tables, and 10 minutes to check your work against the reference answers; this can be completed without an expert. Start with the complete G1 materials on this page and produce calculation, discrepancy/quality-control and handover tables; do not perform real experiments.

Fit signals | U.S. O*NET 19-1029.03 work-activity importance ratings show that getting information (95), documenting and recording information (90), analyzing data or information (89), updating and using relevant knowledge (88), making decisions and solving problems (86), processing information (86), and working with computers (85) are the most important activities in this occupation. Work-context responses indicate daily email use at 96%, daily work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting at 92%, a typical workweek of more than 40 hours at 84%, considerable freedom to make decisions at 64%, exactness or high accuracy being extremely important at 72%, daily face-to-face discussions with individuals or teams at 60%, high competition at 52%, and daily use of common protective or safety equipment at 40%. If you are willing to commit to experiments, research design and data analysis over the long term, maintain rigor and patience in a highly competitive research environment with prolonged uncertainty, manage and share data according to standards, and accept peer review, the daily requirements of this occupation are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | Among respondents, 84% work more than 40 hours per week and 52% report high competition; 28% face strict deadlines at least weekly but not daily, and 36% at least monthly but not weekly. This does not establish that everyone is under sustained high pressure. Check experimental cycles, funding deadlines and protective conditions. Sample mismatches, quality-control failures, overwritten records or use of data beyond its permitted scope may undermine conclusions. Check the ethics, data, clinical and human genetic resource authorizations applicable to the actual activities; pause questionable steps and escalate through institutional procedures.

Editorial suggestion | First complete the three G1 paper draft tables and check 62.5%/50%, 12.5 percentage points, A failing quality control/B being unknown, and the unconfirmed handover. Observe your habits in reading tables, arithmetic and maintaining an audit trail, and list the methods and authorization-related topics to learn next. Real research also requires the relevant training, experimental and statistical skills, ethical and safety safeguards, and lawful authorization; results from 60 minutes cannot demonstrate publishable conclusions, qualifications or long-term fit.

Geneticists study trait inheritance at the molecular, organism or population level. Of the 24 O*NET tasks, 19 core tasks cover literature and methods, research and experiments, statistical interpretation, records, outputs and funding, and team guidance; 5 supplemental tasks include diagnosing and treating genetic disorders. In the actual workflow, check the question, plan and authorization, experimental records, quality-control analysis, review and outputs. Those holding the relevant diagnostic and treatment qualifications may perform clinical tasks within their licensed scope; a research job title itself grants neither diagnostic and treatment authority nor ethics approval authority.

O*NET19-1029.03 Geneticists (2026 profile) studies trait inheritance at the molecular, organism or population level, including supplemental tasks involving licensed evaluation, diagnosis and treatment of genetic disorders. There are 24 tasks, 19 core and 5 supplemental: guidance 87, basic research 85, presenting results 85, notebooks, grant applications/papers and literature/methods 84, reviewing results 83, meetings 82, mathematical/statistical analysis 81, traits 79, and DNA testing 79. Task importance is not working time. Getting information 95, records 90, analysis 89, updating knowledge 88, decisions and information processing 86, and computers 85. Wages, employment and industry shares use the broader 19-1029 group as a proxy. Current projections use the direct BLS 2025–2035 table, rather than separate statistics for geneticists.

entries: Research design and literature support | Hypotheses and methods | Search scientific literature to select and modify the methods and procedures most appropriate for genetic research objectives, propose hypotheses, and design genomic and biological research plans, samples and controls.

Experiments and testing | Operations and records | Conduct research on gene expression regulation, protein interactions, metabolic networks, nucleic acid or protein complexes, and related topics; perform DNA extraction, gel electrophoresis, Southern blotting, polymerase chain reactions and other tests, and maintain laboratory notebooks.

Data and statistical analysis | Calculation and interpretation | Evaluate genetic data using appropriate mathematical or statistical calculations and analysis, analyze factors determining specific inherited traits, and design methods to alter traits or produce new ones.

Interpreting and reviewing results | Quality and uncertainty | Review, approve or interpret genetic laboratory results, assess uncertainties such as data quality, false positives and batch effects, and determine whether repeat or additional experiments are needed.

Producing outputs and securing funding | Papers and projects | Prepare experimental findings for presentation at professional conferences or in scientific journals, write papers and grant applications, or participate in fundraising activities to secure research funding.

Team and clinical collaboration | Guidance and meetings | Supervise or direct the work of other geneticists, biologists, technicians or biostatisticians, attend clinical and research meetings to keep up with technical advances, and provide genetics expertise as arranged by the institution.

Data and integrity | Retain original experimental records, script versions, parameters and statistical plans; when lawfully supplementing or correcting records according to the facts, record the actual time, reason, original value, new value and responsible person, without backdating or overwriting/deleting original evidence. Check the applicable requirements separately for public materials, anonymized materials, human samples and international cooperation; not all research materials are sensitive personal information or human genetic resources.

Records and collaboration | Report anomalous samples, data, authorizations or authorship disputes according to your responsibilities; retain original values and versions, supplement or correct records according to the facts, and indicate the time and basis. Check the authorization of personnel signing off on quality control or clinical matters; do not generate or guess missing experimental steps or backdate signatures.

Boundary conclusion | This page corresponds to U.S. SOC 19-1029.03; the core difference from adjacent roles lies in “outputs and levels of authorization”: this occupation focuses on basic and applied genetics research, experiments and data analysis, producing experimental data, papers, funded projects and research reports; clinical research coordinators (11-9121.01) focus on research-project operations, participant recruitment, data collection and compliance procedures; statisticians (15-2041.00) and biostatisticians focus on statistical methods, experimental design and analysis; bioinformatics technicians (15-2099.01) primarily focus on biological data processing, workflows and tool implementation; molecular and cellular biologists (19-1029.02) focus on mechanisms at the molecular and cellular levels; genetic counselors (29-9092.00) produce genetic risk counseling and consultation reports for patients and families; medical scientists (the 19-1040 series) focus on research related to disease mechanisms and treatment. Outputs and levels of authorization differ; authority for clinical diagnosis and treatment, ethics review or project operations cannot be carried over across roles.

Core principles of adjacent roles | Most roles in the same group and adjacent roles aim to “produce reproducible and interpretable evidence or services through rigorous methods”. Differences lie in their focus, outputs and levels of authorization: some focus on genetics experiments and research conclusions, some on research-project operations and compliance, some on statistical methods and analysis, some on biological data processing and tool implementation, some on molecular and cellular mechanisms, some on patient and family counseling, and some on disease and treatment research.

Core purpose of this occupation | Address genetics questions through research and analysis within the requirements for research ethics, biosafety, human genetic resources, personal data protection and institutional authorization: search literature and design hypotheses and plans; perform experiments and tests and maintain records; conduct statistical and data analysis and interpretation; review and interpret genetic laboratory results; produce papers, grant applications and research reports; guide team members and keep up with technical advances, making research processes and conclusions reproducible and traceable and compliant with integrity and regulatory requirements.

Main focus and basis of adjacent roles | Clinical research coordinators follow requirements for research protocols, participant recruitment, informed consent, data collection, compliance and project operations; statisticians and biostatisticians follow requirements for statistical methodology, experimental design, sample sizes, models and interpretation of results; bioinformatics technicians follow requirements for sequence and omics data processing, workflows, tool implementation and reproducibility; molecular and cellular biologists follow requirements for molecular and cellular mechanism research and experimental models; genetic counselors follow requirements for genetic risk counseling, interpretation of testing information, ethics and informed consent; medical scientists follow requirements for disease-mechanism and treatment research and translation.

Main focus and basis of this occupation | Focus on genetics and genomics research questions, experimental systems, testing methods, raw and processed data, and statistical models, following requirements for research ethics, biosafety, experimental animals, human genetic resources and personal data protection; institutional rules for research, data management, outputs and funding; and collaboration standards with clinical, bioinformatics and statistics teams.

Core process of this occupation | Search literature and define research questions and hypotheses; design experiments, controls, statistics and quality control; obtain ethics, compliance, sample and data approvals; perform experiments and collect raw data; conduct statistical analysis, interpret and review results; maintain records, manage data, produce outputs and apply for funding. Each step must leave an audit trail under institutional research, data and ethics rules and be reviewable by the research team, ethics reviewers and quality-control personnel.

Adjacent outputs | Coordinators primarily implement protocols and manage participants; statistics personnel provide statistical plans, analysis and interpretation; bioinformatics technicians handle data and workflows; molecular and cellular research primarily concerns cells, tissues and functions; counselors explain genetic risks and support family decisions. Collaboration may overlap; the distinction is in main tasks, not an absence of shared research responsibilities.

Main outputs of this occupation | Verifiable laboratory notebooks, raw and processed data, versions and change histories; statistical and analysis records and descriptions of methods; records of review and interpretation of genetic laboratory results; papers, conference abstracts, grant applications and research reports; and records of data/sample management, sharing approvals, project guidance and training.

Responsible parties in adjacent roles | Responsibilities in the same group and adjacent roles are usually defined by the institution, project lead, ethics committee, professional standards and regulations; those responsibilities generally concern research participants, sample providers, projects, institutions and public research integrity.

Responsible parties in this occupation | People in this occupation are responsible for the experiments, data, conclusions, papers and grant materials they design, execute and analyze, and for records, audit trails and sharing approvals completed according to procedures and integrity requirements. Matters involving clinical diagnosis, treatment and medication, ethics review, human genetic resource approval and experimental animal welfare, funding, patents, technology transfer and authorship disputes, and major data or integrity incidents are decided under institutional rules by project leads, ethics committees, institutional research administrators and competent authorities; this occupation does not replace their decisions.

Limits on conclusions in adjacent roles | Conclusions in the same group and adjacent roles are generally limited to the project, method and individual responsibilities, and usually do not constitute determinations of clinical diagnosis, treatment, ethics or forensic evaluation; application across fields or for clinical or evaluation purposes has scope limitations.

Limits on conclusions in this occupation | Research conclusions describe only verifiable experimental conditions, methods, data and analytical results, distinguishing what has been verified, what awaits replication and what requires further analysis. Do not make unauthorized judgments or commitments on matters outside your responsibilities or qualifications, such as clinical diagnosis, treatment plans, ethics determinations or statutory evaluations. Matters involving data anomalies, sample mismatches, suspected contamination, missing approval or informed consent, conflicts of interest or authorship disputes must be paused and escalated or referred; the stated findings must also withstand review by the research team, ethics reviewers, quality-control personnel, funders and regulators.

Checks before joining | Use the following six items for individual checks during application and before joining, to avoid inferring actual responsibilities and authority from job titles or promotional language. Base the findings on written recruitment information, employment contracts, job descriptions, research-team arrangements and ethics/data policy documents, and continue confirming them after joining. This page lists directions for checking, not an official requirements checklist for any institution or research team. Special note: this occupation involves human samples, genetic resources, experimental animals, data and funding; confirm the role’s specific requirements for ethics/compliance approvals, data management, authorship, intellectual property and safety.

Check explanation | Similar job titles may involve very different responsibilities and authority: some primarily involve basic experiments and mechanism research, some clinical genetic testing and result reviews, some data analysis and bioinformatics workflows, some project coordination and compliance, and some translational and industry-collaboration research. Institutions also differ in requirements for project funding sources, authorship rules, sample/data use, responsibilities for ethics and human genetic resource approvals, and safety levels.

01 Actual responsibilities and authorization boundaries | Check whether the role genuinely involves independent research design, experiments, data analysis and interpretation of results, or mainly assistance and workflows; check the permitted scope of sample/data use and its ethics and human genetic resource approval status, materials you may sign and submit and their authorship/intellectual property rules, equipment, biosafety levels and experimental animal permissions, and collaboration and responsibility-routing arrangements with clinical, bioinformatics and statistics teams.

Safety check suggestion | Check chemical, biological or physical hazards, training, protection, exposure response and applicable occupational health requirements according to the actual reagents, equipment, samples and animal activities; the occupational title alone does not establish that all roles involve radiation exposure or the same medical examination requirements.

02 Biosafety, occupational health and experimental animal ethics requirements | Check whether the institution requires and provides: laboratory biosafety-level and operating-procedure training and personal protective equipment; rules on using and disposing of chemical, radiological and biological hazards and reporting exposure; experimental animal welfare, ethics approvals and personnel qualifications; approval and informed-consent procedures for handling human samples and genetic resources; pre-employment and periodic medical examinations and occupational health surveillance; and training in emergency response and reporting for accidents, exposure and sample mismatches.

Check explanation | U.S. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation), with an SVP range of 8.0 and above. The O*NET education survey shows that 36% of respondents indicate postdoctoral training is required, 32% a master’s degree, and 20% a doctoral degree. The BLS education and training table lists a bachelor’s degree as the typical entry-level education, with no related work-experience requirement and no on-the-job training requirement, in the row for broader occupational group 19-1029 (that row covers the broader group; actual education requirements for this occupation are usually higher). This description does not replace employer or competent-authority requirements for qualifications and training.

03 Education, training and skill requirements | Check whether a master’s or doctoral degree in genetics, molecular biology, biochemistry or bioinformatics and postdoctoral experience are required; whether experimental skills such as molecular cloning, sequencing, cell culture and animal experiments, and statistical/programming skills are required; whether relevant professional certification or specialized technical qualifications, such as certification related to clinical genetic testing, are required; whether continuing education and safety refresher training are required; and the institution’s conditions for obtaining authority over independent projects, result reviews, authorship and provision of data to outside parties.

Check explanation | For this occupation, 84% of respondents indicate a typical workweek of more than 40 hours, with periods of high intensity commonly arising from experimental cycles, manuscript submission and grant-application deadlines. Compensation often includes base pay, project or performance payments and publication rewards; obtain written confirmation of hours, performance and assessment criteria, funding and authorship rules.

04 Pay, working hours and contract terms | Check the composition of the offered compensation (base pay, project or role allowances, performance payments or publication/patent rewards), working hours and arrangements for experiments, manuscript submissions and grant applications, probation and assessment criteria (papers, funding and project indicators), and whether arrangements involve intellectual property ownership, income from commercialization of research outputs, confidentiality, noncompete obligations and data ownership.

Check explanation | Interfaces with project leads, clinical teams, laboratories, bioinformatics, statistics, ethics, animal facilities, technical platforms and funders determine responsibility boundaries for research execution, data, authorship and compliance and must be clarified in advance.

05 Authority at interfaces with clinical, bioinformatics, statistics, ethics and technical platforms | Check approval routes for obtaining, using and sharing samples/data; usage and booking rules for experimental equipment, animal facilities and technical platforms; division of work and result-review methods with bioinformatics/statistics personnel; responsibility routing with clinical teams for genetic testing requests and interpretation of results; approval routes with ethics committees for protocol changes, informed consent and data sharing; and reporting routes for data and integrity incidents.

Check explanation | Traceability and audit-trail requirements for laboratory notebooks, raw data, versions, change histories, sharing approvals and authorship records determine research, integrity, ownership and responsibility boundaries. Clarify standards for templates, deadlines, corrections, archiving, permissions and retention periods in advance (human samples and genetic data must also be managed under ethics, human genetic resource and personal information requirements).

Recordkeeping requirements | Check templates, retention periods, access permissions, raw experimental data and analysis versions; corrections must retain the original value, reason, actual time and person making the change. Check authorship against actual contributions and institutional/journal rules; supervisor permission or professional title cannot replace contribution records.

Evidence note | Comparators in the table below come from O*NET occupational classifications and public materials and help distinguish the work and fit of adjacent occupations. They do not establish qualifications, hiring or pay conclusions, and do not constitute research ethics, clinical or legal advice. Wages and employment must be checked separately under each occupation’s own SOC scope; this table makes no numerical comparison and does not use one occupation’s wages as a proxy for another. Check ethics, compliance and authorization boundaries under the relevant jurisdiction and institutional rules.

Introduction | The following comparison uses four columns: “career direction—core work and outputs—key differences—choices it may better suit”. Genetics research, bioinformatics, statistics, clinical research and patient counseling often connect within the same research or healthcare system, but connections do not make roles interchangeable. When moving between directions, learn the methodology, compliance, authorization and responsibility boundaries of the new direction.

Geneticists primarily produce genetics research questions, experimental data and interpretations; coordination, statistics and bioinformatics personnel support project operations, methods and workflows. Collaboration and research responsibilities may overlap; job titles cannot be used to divide parties into groups with no shared responsibility for research conclusions.

May better suit people willing to commit to experiments and data analysis over the long term, maintain rigor and patience amid high competition and prolonged uncertainty, read literature, write papers and grant applications, and continually revise research ideas in response to peer review.

Core work and outputs: search scientific literature to select and modify research methods; plan or conduct basic research related to gene expression regulation, protein interactions, metabolic networks, nucleic acid or protein complexes, and related topics; extract DNA or perform tests such as gel electrophoresis, Southern blotting and polymerase chain reactions; evaluate genetic data and conduct statistical/mathematical analysis; review, approve or interpret genetic laboratory results; maintain laboratory notebooks and manage data; prepare results for professional conferences or journals and write papers and grant applications; outputs include experimental data, papers, funded projects and research reports (U.S. SOC 19-1029.03).
This occupation: geneticists (19-1029.03)

Key difference: clinical research coordinators focus on protocol implementation, participant recruitment and follow-up, data collection, monitoring and compliance, producing project-operation, monitoring and data-collection records; this occupation produces methods, experiments, data analysis and conclusions and usually does not take operational responsibility for participant management and protocol implementation.

May better suit people willing to work in research-project operations, participant communication and compliance-process management; this occupation focuses more on experiments, research design and data analysis.

Core work and outputs: recruit, screen and follow up participants under the protocol; handle informed consent, data collection, entry and verification; coordinate ethics, monitoring and multicenter communication and maintain project logs; outputs include project-operation, monitoring, data-collection and informed-consent records.
Clinical Research Coordinators

Key difference: statisticians and biostatisticians focus on selecting statistical methods, estimating sample sizes for experimental design, models and interpretation of results, producing statistical plans and analysis results; this occupation focuses on genetics experiments, mechanisms and data interpretation, with statistical/mathematical analysis as one component and methodological innovation not its main output.
May better suit people willing to specialize in methodology, statistical inference and experimental design; this occupation focuses more on genetics questions, experiments and mechanisms.

Core work and outputs: design statistical plans, sample sizes, randomization and analysis models; address missing data, multiple comparisons and sensitivity analyses; interpret results and provide methodological suggestions; outputs include statistical plans, analysis results and statistical reports.
Statisticians / Biostatisticians (15-2041.00, among others)

Key difference: bioinformatics technicians focus on processing and aligning sequence and omics data, running workflows, organizing results and implementing tools, producing processed data, workflows and explanations of results; this occupation produces research questions, experiments and conclusions, with bioinformatics analysis as one method and workflow engineering not its primary responsibility.

May better suit people willing to work in data processing, workflows, tools and reproducibility engineering; this occupation focuses more on genetics questions, experiments and conclusions about mechanisms.

Core work and outputs: run and maintain sequence and omics data-processing workflows; perform quality filtering, alignment, annotation and differential analysis; organize and visualize results and communicate with researchers; outputs include processed data, workflows and explanations of results.
Bioinformatics Technicians and similar roles

Key difference: molecular and cellular biologists focus on mechanisms at the molecular and cellular levels, such as cell signaling, gene regulation and protein function, producing conclusions about mechanisms; this occupation focuses more on the genetic basis of traits and diseases and questions at the population, family or genome level.
May better suit people willing to conduct in-depth research on cellular and molecular mechanisms; this occupation focuses more on genetics, genomes and population-level questions.

Core work and outputs: design and conduct cellular and molecular experiments, including culture, transfection, proteins, expression and imaging; verify mechanisms and pathways and write conclusions; outputs include experimental data and conclusions about mechanisms.
Molecular and Cellular Biologists and similar roles

Key difference: genetic counselors produce genetic risk counseling, interpretation of testing information and consultation reports for patients and families, and must work within professional qualifications, ethics and informed-consent boundaries; this occupation produces research, experiments and data and usually does not take responsibility for patient-facing counseling and communication of results (work related to clinical genetic testing follows institutional division of responsibilities and authorization).
May better suit people willing to provide counseling and decision support to patients and families; this occupation focuses more on laboratories, data and research outputs.

paragraphs: Boundary | This page lists relatively common failure types and control points in this occupation’s research design/execution, experiments, data analysis and production of outputs to help identify and manage risks. It is not research ethics, legal or clinical advice or a conclusion on an individual case. Matters involving human samples, genetic resources, experimental animals and biosafety; clinical diagnosis, treatment and interpretation of results; provision of data/samples to outside parties, funding, authorship and intellectual property; and integrity/ethics incidents should be handled by project leads, ethics committees, institutional research administrators and competent authorities under laws and institutional rules. This page describes general research-role situations; specific requirements follow research ethics, biosafety, experimental animal and human genetic resource management regulations and institutional research, data-management and integrity rules.

Direct answer | The core risk in this occupation is not “whether you can conduct experiments”, but five kinds of failures with potentially serious consequences: design/data failures (weak plans, controls or quality control, unidentified sample mismatches or contamination, or inappropriate statistical methods and multiple-comparison handling may make conclusions irreproducible and mislead subsequent research); compliance/ethics failures (missing or exceeded requirements for human samples, genetic resources, experimental animals, informed consent, ethics approvals or human genetic resource approvals may cause compliance and trust consequences); records/integrity failures (false or missing laboratory notebooks/raw data, after-the-fact changes, selective reporting or inappropriate handling of authorship/conflicts of interest affect reproducibility and academic integrity); output/funding failures (unreliable data sources in papers/grant materials, duplicate publication or improper citations affect funding and career development); and data/security failures (leaks, unauthorized access or unauthorized external provision of sensitive sample, genetic or family data may violate personal information, human genetic resource and ethics requirements).

Evidence scope | O*NET19-1029.03: guidance 87, basic research 85, presenting results 85, notebooks, grant applications/papers and literature/methods 84, reviewing results 83, meetings 82, mathematical/statistical analysis 81, DNA testing 79; importance is not working time or risk incidence. Activities: getting information 95, records 90, analysis 89, updating knowledge 88, decisions and information processing 86, computers 85. Contexts: daily email 96%, 84% with workweeks exceeding 40 hours, accuracy extremely important 72%, high competition 52%. Risks and controls below are editorial summaries; check legal and project requirements for the actual subjects and activities.
You, the research team and quality-control roles; research conclusions, subsequent research and participants

Weak plans, controls or quality control, unidentified sample mismatches or contamination, or inappropriate statistical methods and multiple-comparison handling may make conclusions irreproducible, mislead subsequent research and waste resources

Define controls, quality control and statistical plans during design and register the analysis approach in advance; use batch, negative and positive controls during experiments and check sample identifiers. On discovering data anomalies, sample mismatches or suspected contamination, immediately pause, review and repeat

Editorial scenario | A synthetic exercise specifies that the negative control should have no signal, but a positive signal appears; a collaborator urges manuscript submission. First record the quality-control failure and stop interpreting this batch, then request review by project and quality-control leads; do not selectively omit it.
You and the research team, data and quality-control roles; the project, funders and research integrity

Missing or fabricated original records, overwriting without an audit trail or selective reporting may harm reproducibility and integrity; factual corrections with audit trails under institutional rules are a different matter.

Record facts under institutional rules and retain raw data and versions. Corrections must state actual time, reason, original value, new value and responsible person. Backdating, overwriting without an audit trail and selective reporting are prohibited; lawful after-the-fact corrections are not universally prohibited.

Scenario | During handover, you find that the previous shift’s experimental records lack key steps and raw data files, and versions do not match figures/tables; someone suggests filling the gaps from a template.

Leaks, unauthorized access or unauthorized external provision of sensitive human sample, genetic and family data may violate ethics, human genetic resource and personal information requirements and harm the rights and interests of participating parties

Control data according to identifiability, purpose, lawful basis and minimum necessity; de-identification is not anonymization. Check filing, security review and other requirements under the regulations when providing human genetic resource information to foreign parties; general domestic sharing does not universally require the same administrative procedures. Handle leaks immediately through institutional emergency procedures.
Scenario | A stakeholder asks you to send participants’ pedigrees and genetic testing data in an uncontrolled group chat for quick discussion.
You, project leads, ethics and legal roles; the institution and research order

Use of samples/data beyond scope, missing ethics or human genetic resource approvals, or interpreting clinical genetic results beyond authorization may cause compliance, legal, ethical and professional-practice risks

Check ethics review and informed consent for life-science and medical research involving humans. Article 32 of the 2023 measures permits exemption from ethics review for specified situations involving lawfully public data, anonymized information/data, certain existing samples and human-derived cell lines, subject to conditions including no harm to humans and no sensitive personal information or commercial interests; samples and cell lines have additional consent, authorization and exclusion conditions. Check all conditions through institutional procedures: exemption from review does not exempt all consent-related or resource obligations; the human genetic resource regulations do not automatically apply to nonhuman research such as plant research. Administrative approval for human genetic resources in mainland China depends on the activity: Article 4 of the regulations revised in 2024 designates the health department as the competent authority; Article 11 requires approval for collection involving specified families, regions or prescribed types and quantities; Article 14 covers preservation platforms, and Articles 22/27/28 contain separate rules on international cooperation, taking materials abroad and providing information to foreign parties. Do not generalize that every sampling event, ordinary project or domestic sharing requires administrative approval. Physicians’ diagnostic and treatment activities in mainland China require physician qualifications, registration and practice within the authorized scope; specialized techniques such as prenatal diagnosis require separate checks of institutional and personnel conditions. Check U.S. clinical requirements, laboratory certification and state licensing separately. Research titles or O*NET tasks do not grant diagnostic and treatment authority.

Editorial scenario | You are asked to research a new batch of human samples before their purpose, consent and ethics status are clear. Stop using them and check the status with institutional research, ethics and human genetic resource leads; unknown does not mean approved and does not automatically mean that the same human genetic resource filing is required.
You, the research team and technical platforms; project continuity and resources

A single person is responsible for a critical experiment, data or equipment, and research stops during leave, breakdowns or reagent shortages; this may delay progress and affect publication and collaboration

Establish backup and handover rules for experiments, data, equipment and reagents; make key methods, scripts and data reproducible with audit trails. Report staffing or resource shortages under procedures and adjust priorities

Scenario | The only colleague who knows a sequencing and bioinformatics workflow is on leave; the team is asked to have untrained personnel temporarily operate the equipment under that colleague’s telephone guidance.
You, collaborators and funders; projects, outputs and ownership

Unclear delivery and acceptance arrangements for collaborative research, outsourced testing, reagents or data, or inappropriate handling of authorship, intellectual property or conflicts of interest may cause duplicated work, ownership disputes and integrity risks

Collaboration and outsourcing require clear scope, data/sample ownership, acceptance criteria and fee changes with audit trails; disclose and obtain approval for authorship and conflicts of interest under institutional rules. Pause, review and report delivery, ownership or authorship disputes
Scenario | An industry collaborator asks for unpublished data and samples to be shared first and for conclusions to follow its position, while authorship and data ownership have no written agreement.

values: M1 research question (entirely fictional) | Describe only the A allele proportions in groups A and B; do not draw causal conclusions yet. Each synthetic individual is diploid: each AA has 2 A alleles, Aa has 1, and aa has 0; total alleles=2×number of individuals. Random allocation, independent replication, a sampling frame and sample-size power justification are not provided; do not guess them. Significance testing is not required.

M2 raw table v1 (all data) | A01=AA, A02=AA, A03=Aa, A04=aa; B01=AA, B02=Aa, B03=Aa, B04=aa. Both groups contain 4 synthetic individuals. These are observation labels specified by the exercise, not disease diagnoses.

M3 exercise-specific quality-control rules and records | For this exercise only: the negative-control NTC signal must=0. Batch A NTC=8; batch B NTC is unrecorded. Instruments, reagents, experimental steps and replication records are not provided. A cannot be rated as passing, and B’s unknown status cannot be rated as passing; arithmetic can be performed, but the validity of the observations and biological interpretation between groups require verification.

M4 abstract v2 for review | States “group A 6/8=75%, group B 4/8=50%, difference 25 percentage points; each group n=40, treatment caused a genetic mutation, and results can be submitted for publication”. The source provides only M2 v1, without new data, experiments or references; when it conflicts with records, retain the original draft and correct with an audit trail. Do not fabricate literature, samples or experiments.

M5 communication and purposes | This exercise permits paper drafts only; the abstract target is 10:00, with Q checking quality control, versions and release authorization. At 9:40 the draft is marked for review; at 9:43 no confirmation from Q has been received. A third party requests actual human pedigree information, but no such materials, lawful basis or authorization exist; do not send it, call external AI or let approval be given in your place.

M6 draw three tables yourself | ①Data calculations: group, individual ID/genotype, A count, total allele count, proportion, source version; ②Discrepancies and quality control: original draft value, calculated value, discrepancy, basis, status, reviewer; ③Handover: identifier, purpose restrictions, questions to verify, responsible person, sending/confirmation status, actual time. subject.summary: Geneticists correspond to U.S. O*NET/SOC 19-1029.03, “Geneticists”: they research and study the inheritance of traits at the molecular, organism or population level; they may evaluate or treat patients with genetic disorders. Core work includes searching scientific literature to select and modify research methods; planning or conducting basic genomic and biological research related to gene expression regulation, protein interactions, metabolic networks, nucleic acid or protein complexes, and related topics; extracting DNA or performing tests such as gel electrophoresis, Southern blotting and polymerase chain reactions; evaluating genetic data through mathematical or statistical calculations and analysis; reviewing, approving or interpreting genetic laboratory results; maintaining laboratory notebooks and managing data; preparing results for professional conferences or journals and writing papers and grant applications; and supervising or directing the work of other geneticists, biologists, technicians or biostatisticians. Official scope, in the original wording: Research and study the inheritance of traits at the molecular, organism or population level. May evaluate or treat patients with genetic disorders. Wage and employment scope note: the figures displayed by O*NET under this occupation are labelled as covering the broader occupational group 19-1029, “Biological Scientists, All Other”.
